note: Batch A of AI-authored, source-grounded MCQs for the public-policy curriculum's governance, policy design, public finance, programme management, monitoring & evaluation, and impact evaluation competencies, grounded in the DARPG Sevottam guidelines, the NITI Aayog founding resolution, the Fifteenth Finance Commission highlights, the CBC MDO performance-measurement handbook, the Aspirational Districts Programme backgrounder, the DMEO PMGSY evaluation, and UPSC CSP 2023 GS1.

questions.locator: Guideline document title and preamble
questions.source_excerpt: The guideline is titled 'Guidelines for Designing and Implementing SEVOTTAM Compliant Citizen's/Client's Charter & Grievance Redress Mechanism.' 'Sevottam' combines the Hindi words for service ('Seva') and excellence ('Uttam').
questions.question: The DARPG guideline on citizen's/client's charters is built around a service-delivery model called 'Sevottam.' What does the name itself signify?
options: A specific IT platform used to file grievances online
Excellence in service delivery ('Seva' + 'Uttam'), the guiding principle of the model
The name of the committee that drafted India's Right to Information Act
A grading system used only for evaluating passport offices
questions.explanation: 'Sevottam' combines 'Seva' (service) and 'Uttam' (excellence), naming DARPG's citizen-centric service delivery excellence framework. It is not an IT platform, is unrelated to the RTI Act, and is meant to apply across government departments generally, not only passport offices.

questions.locator: Guideline's description of the Sevottam framework's structure
questions.source_excerpt: The Sevottam model comprises three components: Citizen's Charter, Public Grievance Redress Mechanism, and Service Delivery Capability.
questions.question: The Sevottam framework is organised around three components. Which set correctly identifies them?
options: Citizen's Charter, Public Grievance Redress Mechanism, Service Delivery Capability
Right to Information, e-Governance, Digital India
Budget Allocation, Expenditure Audit, Performance Review
Central Vigilance, Lokpal, Ombudsman
questions.explanation: Sevottam's three components are the Citizen's Charter (service standards), the Public Grievance Redress Mechanism (handling complaints), and Service Delivery Capability (organisational readiness to deliver). The other option sets list unrelated governance instruments not part of the model.

questions.locator: Guideline's discussion of the Citizen's Charter component
questions.source_excerpt: A Citizen's Charter states the services a department provides, the standards it commits to, and how grievances will be addressed.
questions.question: Within the Sevottam framework, what is the primary function of the Citizen's Charter component?
options: To fix the annual budget ceiling for a department
To publicly declare the services offered, the standards committed to, and how complaints will be handled
To assign disciplinary action against non-performing officials
To determine promotion criteria for civil servants
questions.explanation: A Citizen's Charter is a public commitment listing the services provided, measurable service standards, and the grievance-handling process, so citizens know what to expect. It is not a budgeting, disciplinary, or promotion instrument.

questions.locator: Guideline's section on grievance redress
questions.source_excerpt: The grievance redress mechanism is meant to receive, register, investigate, and work toward a satisfactory resolution of citizen complaints within a defined process.
questions.question: A citizen submits a complaint about a delayed service under a department's Sevottam-compliant grievance mechanism. Which of the following best reflects how the Public Grievance Redress Mechanism (PGRM) is meant to function?
options: It ignores complaints unless they are submitted in person at the head office
It receives, registers, investigates, and works toward a satisfactory resolution of the complaint within a defined process
It refers every complaint automatically to a court of law
It only applies to complaints about corruption, not about service delays
questions.explanation: The PGRM is an administrative process for receiving, recording, investigating and resolving citizen grievances -- including delays -- within set timelines, not a judicial referral system, and it is not restricted to corruption complaints or in-person submissions.

questions.locator: Guideline's section on Service Delivery Capability
questions.source_excerpt: Service Delivery Capability includes the standard operating procedures, staff orientation/training, and infrastructure needed to meet the charter's commitments.
questions.question: A department has published an ambitious Citizen's Charter promising fast turnaround times, but its Sevottam compliance assessment flags it as deficient in 'Service Delivery Capability.' What does this most likely mean?
options: The department has not yet translated its charter's promises into the standard operating procedures, trained staff, and infrastructure needed to actually deliver on them
The department has not registered its charter with the Ministry of Finance
The department's charter uses too many languages for citizens to understand
The department has exceeded its promised standards and needs to lower them
questions.explanation: Service Delivery Capability is the internal readiness -- processes, trained staff, systems, infrastructure -- needed to meet what the Citizen's Charter promises. A charter with ambitious promises but weak capability shows good intentions outrunning operational readiness; the other options describe unrelated or implausible issues.

questions.locator: Guideline's discussion of the underlying service-standard-setting cycle
questions.source_excerpt: The underlying approach requires organisations to define services and clients, set standards, build capability, perform, monitor, evaluate independently, and improve.
questions.question: Sevottam's underlying model treats a citizen's charter not as a one-time document but as a repeating cycle. Which sequence best matches that cycle's logic?
options: Publish the charter once, then leave it unchanged indefinitely
Define services and clients, set standards, build capability, perform, monitor performance, evaluate impact, and feed lessons back into improvement
Set standards only after an independent audit is complete
Skip standard-setting and jump directly to grievance redress
questions.explanation: The model behind Sevottam-compliant charters is cyclical: define what is delivered and to whom, set standards, build the capability to meet them, deliver, monitor and independently evaluate performance, and feed lessons back into improvement -- not a static, one-time publication, nor a sequence that skips standard-setting.

questions.locator: Resolution's preamble
questions.source_excerpt: The Cabinet Secretariat Resolution dated 1 January 2015 constitutes NITI Aayog in place of the Planning Commission.
questions.question: The Cabinet Secretariat's Resolution of 1 January 2015 constituted NITI Aayog. Which institution did it replace?
options: The Finance Commission
The Planning Commission
The Election Commission
The Union Public Service Commission
questions.explanation: The 1 January 2015 resolution dissolved the Planning Commission, which had existed since 1950, and replaced it with NITI Aayog. It did not touch the Finance Commission, Election Commission, or UPSC, which are separate constitutional/statutory bodies.

questions.locator: Resolution's stated rationale for the new institution
questions.source_excerpt: The resolution reorients national planning away from the Planning Commission's more centralised approach toward cooperative federalism, with States actively involved in shaping national priorities.
questions.question: The resolution frames NITI Aayog's creation as part of a shift in how the Union government engages with States on development planning. What is that shift best described as?
options: A move from cooperative federalism back toward central planning targets
A move from a centralised, top-down planning model toward a cooperative-federalism model with States as active partners
A move to abolish all Union-State consultation on development
A move to transfer all planning powers entirely to individual states with no central coordination
questions.explanation: The resolution reorients national planning away from the Planning Commission's more centralised approach toward 'cooperative federalism,' with States actively involved in shaping national priorities -- not abolishing coordination, reversing the shift, or removing the Centre's role entirely.

questions.locator: Resolution's listed objectives
questions.source_excerpt: To evolve a shared vision of national development priorities, sectors and strategies with the active involvement of States in the light of national objectives.
questions.question: One objective in the resolution reads: 'To evolve a shared vision of national development priorities, sectors and strategies with the active involvement of States...'. What does this objective primarily commit NITI Aayog to?
options: Setting national priorities unilaterally and informing States afterward
Co-developing national development priorities together with State governments rather than dictating them centrally
Delegating all priority-setting entirely to individual States with no national-level vision
Limiting States' role to implementation only, with no input into priority-setting
questions.explanation: The objective explicitly calls for a 'shared vision' developed 'with the active involvement of States' -- a collaborative process, not a unilateral, delegated, or implementation-only role for States.

questions.locator: Resolution's institutional design -- Governing Council
questions.source_excerpt: NITI Aayog's Governing Council comprises the Chief Ministers of all States and Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories, chaired by the Prime Minister.
questions.question: NITI Aayog's Governing Council includes the Chief Ministers of all States and the Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories, chaired by the Prime Minister. Why is this composition significant for governance design?
options: It ensures every major policy decision is made without any State input
It institutionalises direct, regular participation of State political leadership in national policy deliberation, rather than routing it only through bureaucratic channels
It removes the Prime Minister from any role in national planning
It replaces the need for any Union ministries to be involved in development planning
questions.explanation: Putting all Chief Ministers and UT Lt. Governors on the Governing Council under the Prime Minister's chairmanship builds direct political-level Centre-State engagement into the institution's design -- the opposite of excluding State input, and it does not remove the PM or the ministries from the process.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on national security and economic strategy
questions.source_excerpt: To ensure, on areas that are specifically referred to it, that the interests of national security are incorporated in economic strategy and policy.
questions.question: The resolution assigns NITI Aayog a role in ensuring national security interests are incorporated into economic strategy and policy, for matters referred to it. What does this reveal about the intended scope of the institution?
options: It is meant to function purely as a fiscal auditor with no role beyond budget-checking
Its policy-advisory mandate extends beyond conventional economic planning to cross-cutting concerns such as national security, when specifically referred
It has been given command authority over the armed forces
It replaces the National Security Council in all matters
questions.explanation: This objective shows NITI Aayog's advisory remit was designed to be broader than routine economic planning, covering cross-cutting concerns like national security when a matter is referred to it -- but it grants no military command authority and does not replace the National Security Council.

questions.locator: Resolution's listed objectives
questions.source_excerpt: To pay special attention to the sections of our society that may be at risk of not benefitting adequately from economic progress.
questions.question: Among NITI Aayog's stated objectives is paying special attention to groups 'at risk of not benefitting adequately from economic progress.' Which governance principle does this most directly reflect?
options: Fiscal austerity above all other considerations
Inclusive governance -- ensuring economic growth's benefits reach vulnerable and marginalised groups, not just the already well-off
Strict market deregulation as the primary development strategy
Centralising all welfare spending decisions in one ministry
questions.explanation: This objective reflects a commitment to inclusive governance: actively watching for and addressing groups that growth might otherwise bypass. It is not primarily about austerity, deregulation, or centralising welfare administration.

questions.locator: Examination's overall structure and purpose
questions.source_excerpt: The paper is an objective-type General Studies paper covering polity, governance, economy, and current affairs, used to screen candidates for the civil services.
questions.question: The UPSC Civil Services (Preliminary) Examination's General Studies Paper I is an objective-type test covering polity, governance, economy, geography, and current affairs. What is its primary institutional purpose?
options: To directly appoint candidates to specific ministries without further stages
To screen candidates' general awareness and reasoning ability as an initial stage before the Mains examination and interview for recruitment to the civil services
To evaluate candidates only on their handwriting and language skills
To replace the need for an interview stage entirely
questions.explanation: GS Paper I of the Preliminary examination is a screening stage -- testing general awareness and analytical ability -- before candidates proceed to the Mains written examination and the Personality Test. It is not itself a final appointment or a skills-only test, and it does not eliminate the interview stage.

questions.locator: 2023 paper's item on prison administration
questions.source_excerpt: Prisons in India are managed by State Governments and governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 -- a topic tested in the 2023 paper.
questions.question: One of the 2023 paper's questions concerns how prisons in India are administered. Which statement correctly reflects that governance arrangement?
options: Prisons are managed exclusively by the Union Home Ministry with no State role
Prisons are managed by State Governments and governed under a colonial-era statute, the Prisons Act, 1894
Prisons are managed by the judiciary directly, bypassing the executive
There is no statutory framework governing prisons in India
questions.explanation: Prison administration in India is a State subject, carried out by State Governments, with the Prisons Act, 1894 as the foundational statute -- not a Union-only function, not judiciary-run, and not without a statutory basis.

questions.locator: 2023 paper's item on the Production-Linked Incentive scheme
questions.source_excerpt: The paper tests awareness of the Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, a Union government instrument to boost domestic manufacturing.
questions.question: The 2023 paper includes a question on India's 'Production-Linked Incentive' (PLI) scheme. As a governance instrument, what is the PLI scheme designed to do?
options: Provide financial incentives to companies based on their incremental domestic production/sales, to boost domestic manufacturing and reduce import dependence
Provide a fixed subsidy to every registered company regardless of output
Directly nationalise private manufacturing units
Waive all import duties on finished consumer goods
questions.explanation: PLI schemes tie government incentive payouts to a company's incremental production or sales performance in targeted sectors, aiming to boost domestic manufacturing and reduce import dependence -- not a flat unconditional subsidy, nationalisation, or a blanket duty waiver.

questions.locator: 2023 paper's item on the G20
questions.source_excerpt: The paper tests that the G20 serves as a platform where Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors of member countries discuss international economic and financial issues.
questions.question: The 2023 paper tests knowledge of the G20 grouping. In its original conception, what was the G20 primarily created as a platform for?
options: Military coordination between member nations
Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors of member countries to discuss international economic and financial issues
Resolving territorial disputes between member states
Selecting the head of the United Nations
questions.explanation: The G20 originated as a forum for Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors to discuss international economic and financial stability, later expanding to Leaders' Summits -- its founding purpose was economic/financial coordination, not military, territorial, or UN-related matters.

questions.locator: Resolution's rationale for establishing NITI Aayog
questions.source_excerpt: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission, which had allocated central plan funds to states, and was instead designed as an advisory think tank.
questions.question: The resolution replaced the Planning Commission -- which had allocated central plan funds to states -- with NITI Aayog, designed instead as an advisory think tank. What does this shift in institutional design represent?
options: A shift from a fund-allocating planning body to a policy-advisory, think-tank model without direct control over plan funds
No real change -- NITI Aayog retained identical fund-allocation powers
A shift that gave NITI Aayog control over the entire Union Budget
A shift that abolished all central planning functions permanently
questions.explanation: NITI Aayog was deliberately designed without the Planning Commission's power to allocate plan funds, functioning instead as an advisory/think-tank body -- a genuine design change, not a continuation of the old allocative role, and not a takeover of the Union Budget or an end to planning altogether.

questions.locator: Resolution's first listed objective
questions.source_excerpt: To evolve a shared vision of national development priorities, sectors and strategies with the active involvement of States in the light of national objectives.
questions.question: From a policy-design standpoint, why does the resolution insist that national development priorities be evolved 'with the active involvement of States' rather than being fixed centrally and merely communicated to them?
options: Because policies designed without buy-in from the implementing states risk poor ownership and weak on-the-ground implementation
Because the Constitution legally prohibits any central role in planning
Because States have no relevant information to contribute to policy design
Because it was purely a symbolic gesture with no bearing on implementation
questions.explanation: Involving States early in shaping priorities builds ownership and reflects on-the-ground realities that implementing governments know best -- policies designed top-down without such buy-in typically face weaker implementation. States clearly have relevant local knowledge, and the resolution treats this as a substantive design choice, not a symbolic one.

questions.locator: Resolution's second listed objective
questions.source_excerpt: To foster cooperative federalism through structured support initiatives and mechanisms with the States on a continuous basis, recognising that strong States make a strong nation.
questions.question: The objective on cooperative federalism describes 'structured support initiatives and mechanisms with the States on a continuous basis.' What does 'continuous' signal about how this objective was meant to be designed, as opposed to a one-off consultation?
options: An ongoing, sustained engagement process rather than a single consultative event
A process that only occurs once every five years, matching the old Five-Year Plans
A process limited to written correspondence with no institutional mechanism
A process that ends once a State's plan document is approved
questions.explanation: Describing the support as 'continuous' signals an ongoing engagement mechanism, not a single event, a rigid five-year cycle carried over from the old planning model, or a process that terminates upon approval of a document.

questions.locator: Resolution's third listed objective
questions.source_excerpt: To develop mechanisms to formulate credible plans at the village level and aggregate these progressively at higher levels of government.
questions.question: The resolution calls for plans to be formulated 'at the village level' and then 'aggregated progressively at higher levels.' As a policy-design approach, what does this represent?
options: A top-down approach where national targets are broken down and imposed on villages
A bottom-up approach where local-level plans build upward to inform higher-level (state and national) planning
An approach that excludes village-level input entirely from national planning
An approach applicable only to urban municipal planning
questions.explanation: Building plans starting at the village level and aggregating them upward is explicitly a bottom-up design, the opposite of a top-down target-imposition model -- and it is described for village-level (rural) planning, not limited to urban municipalities, nor does it exclude local input.

questions.locator: Resolution's fourth listed objective
questions.source_excerpt: To ensure, on areas that are specifically referred to it, that the interests of national security are incorporated in economic strategy and policy.
questions.question: Why might a policy-design resolution explicitly call out incorporating 'national security' interests into economic strategy, rather than treating economic and security policy as entirely separate domains?
options: Because good policy design recognises that some economic decisions (e.g. strategic industries, border-area development) have security implications that need to be factored in during design, not as an afterthought
Because national security concerns automatically override every economic consideration in all circumstances
Because the resolution intends to merge the Ministry of Defence into the economic planning body
Because this is a purely ceremonial clause with no design implication
questions.explanation: Explicitly naming national security as a design consideration reflects an understanding that certain economic choices carry security implications worth weighing during policy design -- a factor to incorporate, not an automatic override, no institutional merger with Defence, and a substantive rather than ceremonial clause.

questions.locator: Resolution's fifth listed objective
questions.source_excerpt: To pay special attention to the sections of our society that may be at risk of not benefitting adequately from economic progress.
questions.question: In designing a theory of change for national development, why would a planning body explicitly build in a step to identify groups 'at risk of not benefitting adequately' from growth, rather than assuming growth benefits everyone equally?
options: Because economic growth does not automatically translate into equal benefits for all groups, so a deliberate equity check is needed in the design
Because it is a legal requirement with no connection to actual outcomes
Because such groups do not exist in a growing economy
Because this step replaces the need for any economic growth strategy at all
questions.explanation: Growth does not automatically distribute benefits evenly, so a deliberate design step to identify and support at-risk groups reflects equity-aware policy design -- not a symbolic legal box-tick, and it does not deny such groups exist or substitute for a growth strategy but complements it.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on strategic and long-term policy frameworks
questions.source_excerpt: To design strategic and long term policy and programme frameworks and initiatives, and monitor their progress and their efficacy.
questions.question: This objective pairs 'designing' policy frameworks with a duty to 'monitor their progress and efficacy.' Why is bundling design and monitoring into a single institutional mandate significant for policy design?
options: It closes the loop between designing a policy and learning whether it actually works, rather than treating design and evaluation as unconnected activities
It means the institution designs policy but is legally barred from ever reviewing it again
It means monitoring happens only once, at the very start of a policy's life
It has no bearing on how policies are eventually revised
questions.explanation: Combining design and monitoring in one mandate builds a feedback loop -- an institution that designs a policy is also responsible for tracking whether it works -- rather than being barred from revisiting it, doing a one-time check, or being disconnected from eventual policy revision.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on resolving inter-sectoral and inter-departmental issues
questions.source_excerpt: To provide a platform for resolution of inter-sectoral and inter-departmental issues in order to accelerate the implementation of the development agenda.
questions.question: Two ministries disagree over overlapping responsibilities for a rural infrastructure scheme, stalling its rollout. Which of NITI Aayog's stated design objectives is most directly meant to address a situation like this?
options: Its role as a platform for resolving inter-sectoral and inter-departmental issues to accelerate implementation
Its objective to pay special attention to at-risk sections of society
Its objective to incorporate national security interests into economic strategy
Its role in fostering cooperative federalism with States
questions.explanation: The resolution specifically designs NITI Aayog to serve as a coordination platform for resolving inter-sectoral/inter-departmental disputes so implementation is not stalled -- the other listed objectives address equity, security, and Centre-State relations rather than inter-ministerial coordination.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on maintaining a resource centre
questions.source_excerpt: To provide a resource centre for research on good governance and best practices in sustainable and equitable development as well as help their dissemination to stake-holders.
questions.question: The resolution tasks NITI Aayog with maintaining a 'resource centre' on good governance and best practices for dissemination to stakeholders. What role does this play in policy design across the country?
options: It positions NITI Aayog as a knowledge-sharing hub so that successful approaches in one state can inform policy design elsewhere, rather than each state reinventing solutions in isolation
It restricts research findings to internal government use only, with no external dissemination
It requires every state to adopt identical policies regardless of local context
It replaces the need for any state-specific policy research
questions.explanation: A resource centre that disseminates best practices spreads learning across states so good ideas travel, rather than being reinvented independently everywhere -- it is meant for dissemination, does not force uniform policy, and does not eliminate the need for local research.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on national and international partnerships
questions.source_excerpt: To provide a platform for national and international partnerships towards sustainable development goals.
questions.question: Why would the body responsible for domestic development planning also be given an explicit objective to build 'national and international partnerships towards sustainable development goals'?
options: Because development challenges (e.g. climate, poverty) often require external expertise, funding, or coordinated global commitments that a purely domestic body could not access alone
Because it removes any role for India's Ministry of External Affairs in development matters
Because domestic development goals have no connection to global sustainable development frameworks
Because international partnerships were meant only for defence cooperation
questions.explanation: Linking domestic planning to international partnerships lets the institution draw on external expertise, funding and globally coordinated commitments that purely domestic action cannot fully deliver -- it does not sideline the Ministry of External Affairs, and domestic and global development goals are explicitly connected, not unrelated.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on technology upgradation and capacity building
questions.source_excerpt: To focus on technology upgradation and capacity building for implementation of programmes and initiatives.
questions.question: A well-designed policy can still fail if the implementing agency lacks the technical skills or systems to execute it. Which of the resolution's objectives is aimed directly at preventing that kind of implementation failure?
options: Its objective to focus on technology upgradation and capacity building for implementation of programmes and initiatives
Its objective to incorporate national security interests into economic strategy
Its objective to pay special attention to at-risk sections of society
Its objective to foster cooperative federalism with structured support mechanisms
questions.explanation: The objective on technology upgradation and capacity building is specifically about building the operational capability needed to execute programmes well -- directly addressing implementation gaps, unlike the equity-, security-, or federalism-focused objectives.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective describing NITI Aayog as a think tank
questions.source_excerpt: To actualise the vision of the Prime Minister to provide a critical directional and strategic input into the development process, functioning as a think tank that provides governments at the central and state levels with relevant strategic and technical advice.
questions.question: The resolution describes NITI Aayog as functioning as a 'think tank' providing 'directional and strategic input,' in contrast to the Planning Commission's earlier role of directly allocating plan funds. What is the key design trade-off in choosing an advisory think-tank model over a fund-allocating one?
options: The think-tank model gains flexibility to advise broadly and adapt to changing priorities, but trades away the direct financial leverage the old model used to compel state compliance
There is no trade-off -- the think-tank model retains identical financial leverage over states
The think-tank model gives NITI Aayog binding legislative power over states
The think-tank model removes any need for the institution to engage with states at all
questions.explanation: An advisory think-tank can be more flexible and issue-responsive, but it gives up the direct budgetary lever the Planning Commission held over states -- a genuine design trade-off, not a costless equivalence, and it grants no legislative power or excuse to disengage from states.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on encouraging partnerships with think tanks and research institutions
questions.source_excerpt: To provide advice and encourage partnerships between key stakeholders and national and international like-minded Think Tanks, as well as educational and policy research institutions.
questions.question: Why does the resolution explicitly encourage partnerships with 'national and international...Think Tanks, as well as educational and policy research institutions' rather than relying solely on internal government expertise for policy design?
options: Because external research and academic institutions can bring specialised, independent analysis that broadens and strengthens the evidence base behind policy choices
Because government officials are legally barred from doing any policy analysis themselves
Because think tanks are given final decision-making authority over government policy
Because this objective applies only to foreign governments, not research institutions
questions.explanation: Bringing in external think tanks and research institutions widens the pool of specialised, independent analysis feeding into policy design -- it supplements rather than replaces internal capacity, does not hand think tanks decision-making authority, and covers both national and international, think-tank and academic, institutions.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on creating a knowledge and innovation hub
questions.source_excerpt: To create a knowledge, innovation and entrepreneurial support system through a collaborative community of national and international experts, practitioners and other partners.
questions.question: One objective envisions NITI Aayog helping create a 'knowledge, innovation and entrepreneurial support system through a collaborative community' of experts and practitioners. What kind of policy-design function does this describe?
options: Convening a network that connects experts, practitioners, and partners so ideas and innovations can be surfaced and channelled into policy, rather than the institution generating all ideas internally
Directly funding start-up companies as venture capital investments
Replacing India's universities with a single central research body
Restricting policy input to only serving central government employees
questions.explanation: This objective is about convening a broad collaborative network to surface knowledge and innovation for policy use, not about acting as a venture-capital fund, replacing universities, or limiting input to internal government staff.

questions.locator: Resolution's section on NITI Aayog's composition
questions.source_excerpt: The Governing Council comprises the Chief Ministers of all States and Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories.
questions.question: As a matter of institutional design, who sits on NITI Aayog's Governing Council alongside the Prime Minister as Chairperson?
options: Only the Union Cabinet Ministers
The Chief Ministers of all States and Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories
Only the Chief Ministers of States ruled by the same party as the Union government
Only District Magistrates nominated by the Union Home Ministry
questions.explanation: The Governing Council is designed to include the Chief Ministers of all States and the Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories -- a deliberately inclusive, party-neutral design -- not limited to Union ministers, ruling-party-aligned states, or district-level officials.

questions.locator: Resolution's provision for Regional Councils
questions.source_excerpt: Regional Councils will be formed to address specific issues and contingencies impacting more than one state or a region, comprising Chief Ministers of States and Lt. Governors of UTs, convened by the Prime Minister for a specified tenure.
questions.question: The resolution provides for 'Regional Councils' to address issues affecting more than one State or a region, convened by the Prime Minister for a specified tenure. What policy-design problem does this mechanism solve?
options: It creates a flexible, time-bound consultative structure for cross-boundary issues that don't fit neatly within a single state's jurisdiction or the full Governing Council's broad national agenda
It permanently replaces the Governing Council for all decision-making
It removes the need for the Prime Minister's involvement in regional issues
It applies only to disputes between two central ministries, not states
questions.explanation: Regional Councils give the institution a flexible, tenure-bound mechanism to tackle issues spanning multiple states or a region -- filling a gap between single-state matters and the full national Governing Council agenda -- rather than replacing the Council, excluding the PM, or being limited to inter-ministerial disputes.

questions.locator: Resolution's provision on part-time members
questions.source_excerpt: Part time members: maximum of 2, from leading universities, research organisations and other relevant institutions in an ex-officio capacity, on a rotational basis.
questions.question: The resolution allows up to two 'part-time members' drawn from leading universities and research organisations, serving on a rotational basis. What design purpose does rotating part-time academic membership serve, compared to permanent full-time appointments only?
options: It lets the institution periodically refresh its access to current academic and technical expertise without permanently embedding any single set of external individuals in government
It ensures the same two academics remain on the body for life
It removes any role for external experts, keeping the body purely bureaucratic
It only allows retired judges to serve in these roles
questions.explanation: Rotating part-time membership lets NITI Aayog periodically draw in fresh academic/technical expertise without permanently fixing who holds those seats -- the opposite of lifetime tenure, of excluding external experts, or of restricting the role to retired judges.

questions.locator: Resolution's provision on the Chief Executive Officer
questions.source_excerpt: Chief Executive Officer: to be appointed by the Prime Minister for a fixed tenure, in the rank of Secretary to the Government of India.
questions.question: The resolution specifies that NITI Aayog's Chief Executive Officer is appointed by the Prime Minister for a fixed tenure, at the rank of Secretary to the Government of India. Why does giving the CEO a defined tenure and a specific administrative rank matter for the institution's functioning?
options: A fixed tenure and clear administrative rank give the CEO the standing to coordinate with other government departments and provide continuity and stability in running the organisation's day-to-day work
It ensures the CEO position is only symbolic, with no actual administrative responsibility
It gives the CEO higher authority than the Prime Minister on all matters
It ties the CEO's tenure to the term of a specific State's Chief Minister
questions.explanation: Fixing the CEO's tenure and pegging their rank to Secretary-level gives them recognised standing to work across government machinery, plus administrative continuity -- it does not make the role symbolic, does not place the CEO above the Prime Minister, and has no link to any State Chief Minister's term.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's key highlights on the divisible pool
questions.source_excerpt: The Commission recommended that States' share in the central divisible pool of taxes be maintained at 41% for the 2021-26 period.
questions.question: What share of the central divisible pool of taxes did the Fifteenth Finance Commission recommend devolving to States for the 2021-26 award period?
questions.explanation: The Fifteenth Finance Commission recommended a vertical devolution of 41% of the divisible pool of central taxes to States for 2021-26. The other figures do not match its recommendation.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's explanation of the change from the Fourteenth Finance Commission's recommendation
questions.source_excerpt: The recommended 41% share is about 1 percentage point lower than the Fourteenth Finance Commission's 42%, adjusted to account for the changed status of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh as Union Territories.
questions.question: The Fifteenth Finance Commission's 41% vertical devolution share is about one percentage point lower than the Fourteenth Finance Commission's 42%. What explains this specific adjustment?
options: A reduction to account for Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh becoming Union Territories, which are funded directly from the Union's resources rather than through State devolution
A punitive cut applied because States failed to meet fiscal deficit targets
An increase, not a decrease, was actually recommended
A change unrelated to any administrative reorganisation
questions.explanation: The roughly 1-percentage-point reduction reflects the reorganisation of Jammu & Kashmir into two Union Territories, no longer eligible for the State share of devolution and instead funded from Union resources -- not a punitive fiscal measure, and the change was a decrease, not an increase.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's table of horizontal devolution criteria
questions.source_excerpt: Criteria and weights for horizontal devolution include income distance (45%), area (15%), population 2011 (15%), demographic performance (12.5%), forest and ecology (10%), and tax and fiscal efforts (2.5%).
questions.question: Among the Fifteenth Finance Commission's horizontal devolution criteria for distributing funds among States, which criterion carries the single largest weight?
options: Population (2011)
Income distance
Forest and ecology
Tax and fiscal efforts
questions.explanation: Income distance -- how far a State's per-capita income lies from the State with the highest per-capita income -- carries the largest weight (45%), reflecting an equity-focused emphasis on need. Population, forest cover, and tax effort each carry smaller weights.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's description of the income distance criterion
questions.source_excerpt: Income distance measures the gap between a State's per-capita income and that of the State with the highest per-capita income.
questions.question: The 'income distance' criterion, weighted at 45% in horizontal devolution, is based on the gap between a State's per-capita income and that of the State with the highest per-capita income. What principle does this criterion embody?
options: Equity -- poorer states (with a larger income gap) receive proportionately more, to help offset income disparities across states
Population control -- rewarding states that reduced their birth rates
Environmental protection -- rewarding states with more forest cover
Fiscal discipline -- rewarding states that collect more of their own tax revenue
questions.explanation: Income distance is an equity criterion: states further behind the richest state in per-capita income receive a larger share, narrowing disparities. It has nothing to do with population control, forests, or own-tax effort, which are separate criteria.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's description of the demographic performance criterion
questions.source_excerpt: The demographic performance criterion rewards States for their performance on population-related indicators, using a reference period distinct from the raw 2011 Census population figure.
questions.question: The demographic performance criterion (weight 12.5%) is meant to reward States for their performance on population-related indicators. What does this criterion primarily recognise?
options: States' efforts in managing population growth/fertility, using a reference period distinct from the raw 2011 Census population figure
The absolute size of a State's population, favouring the most populous States
The percentage of a State's population living in forested areas
How much foreign direct investment a State has attracted
questions.explanation: The demographic performance criterion rewards states for controlling population growth, using demographic indicators rather than simply favouring the largest population -- distinct from the separate 'population (2011)' criterion, and unrelated to forest cover or FDI.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's description of the forest and ecology criterion
questions.source_excerpt: The forest and ecology criterion compensates States with large forest cover for the development opportunities they forgo through conservation.
questions.question: The forest and ecology criterion (weight 10%) in horizontal devolution is intended to do what?
options: Compensate States with large forest cover for the development opportunities they forgo by conserving forest land
Penalise States that have any forest cover at all
Reward States purely based on total geographical area, regardless of land use
Fund only afforestation projects directly, bypassing State budgets entirely
questions.explanation: This criterion recognises that States with extensive forest cover bear an opportunity cost -- restricted industrial/agricultural development -- for conservation, and compensates them accordingly, rather than penalising forest cover, rewarding raw area regardless of land use, or bypassing state budgets.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's description of the tax and fiscal effort criterion
questions.source_excerpt: The tax and fiscal effort criterion rewards States for a stronger relative effort in mobilising their own tax revenues.
questions.question: The tax and fiscal effort criterion (weight 2.5%) in horizontal devolution rewards States for what?
options: Demonstrating stronger effort in mobilising their own tax revenues, relative to their fiscal capacity
Spending the largest absolute amount on capital expenditure
Having the lowest population growth in the country
Maintaining the largest area of protected forest land
questions.explanation: The tax and fiscal effort criterion rewards states that make a stronger relative effort to raise their own tax revenues -- fiscal discipline and effort -- rather than rewarding capital spending totals, low population growth, or forest cover, which are separate criteria.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's section on local government grants
questions.source_excerpt: The Commission recommended grants to local governments -- rural and urban local bodies -- alongside State-level tax devolution.
questions.question: Beyond the formula-based devolution, the Fifteenth Finance Commission also recommended grants to local governments (rural and urban bodies). What is the primary rationale for such grants existing alongside State-level devolution?
options: To strengthen fiscal resources at the third tier of government (panchayats and municipalities), which formula-based devolution to States does not directly address
To eliminate the need for any State-level government spending
To fund only central government office buildings in state capitals
To replace the State Finance Commissions entirely
questions.explanation: Local government grants target the third tier -- panchayats and municipalities -- ensuring fiscal resources reach local bodies directly, which state-level devolution formulas do not guarantee; they do not eliminate state spending, fund only central offices, or replace State Finance Commissions.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's section on revenue deficit grants
questions.source_excerpt: Revenue deficit grants address a projected gap between a State's assessed revenue receipts (including its share of devolution) and its assessed revenue expenditure.
questions.question: Revenue deficit grants recommended by the Commission are meant to address what specific fiscal situation for eligible States?
options: A projected gap between a State's assessed revenue receipts (including its share of devolution) and its assessed revenue expenditure
A surplus in a State's capital account
A shortfall in central government's own tax collection
A dispute between two States over a shared river's water allocation
questions.explanation: Revenue deficit grants bridge the gap for States whose assessed revenue expenditure exceeds their assessed revenue receipts (post-devolution) -- not a capital surplus, a central government shortfall, or an inter-state water dispute, which are handled through entirely different mechanisms.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's section on disaster management grants
questions.source_excerpt: The Commission's disaster management grants framework distinguishes funding for mitigation and for response.
questions.question: The Commission's recommendations on disaster management grants continue a framework built around funds for both mitigation and response. What is the key distinction between 'mitigation' and 'response' funding in this framework?
options: Mitigation funding supports measures to reduce disaster risk before it strikes, while response funding supports relief and recovery after a disaster occurs
Mitigation funding is only for earthquakes, while response funding is only for floods
Both terms mean exactly the same thing and are interchangeable
Mitigation funding is provided only to the Union government, never to States
questions.explanation: Mitigation funds support pre-disaster risk-reduction measures, while response funds support relief and recovery once a disaster has occurred -- a substantive distinction in purpose and timing, not interchangeable terms, not hazard-specific, and States do receive disaster management funding.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's section on sector-specific, state-specific, and performance grants
questions.source_excerpt: Alongside formula-based tax devolution, the Commission recommended sector-specific grants (e.g. health, education), state-specific grants, and performance-based incentives.
questions.question: Alongside formula-based tax devolution, the Commission recommended sector-specific grants (e.g. health, education), state-specific grants, and performance-based incentives. Why does a Finance Commission use these additional, more targeted instruments rather than relying only on the general devolution formula?
options: Because a single general formula cannot address every state's unique circumstances or incentivise specific policy priorities and reform performance the way targeted grants can
Because targeted grants are legally required to be smaller than the vertical devolution share in every case
Because sector-specific grants replace the need for any general devolution formula
Because performance-based incentives are given equally to every state regardless of performance
questions.explanation: General devolution formulas are necessarily broad and cannot capture every state's specific needs or reward specific reform efforts, which is why targeted grants exist alongside them -- these complement rather than replace the general formula, and performance incentives are tied to actual performance, not distributed equally regardless of it.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's overall framework of devolution plus grants
questions.source_excerpt: The Commission's recommendations combine formula-based vertical/horizontal devolution with a layered system of local government, revenue deficit, disaster, sector-specific, state-specific and performance grants.
questions.question: Taken together, the Fifteenth Finance Commission's design -- a formula-based vertical/horizontal devolution plus a layered system of local government, revenue deficit, disaster, sector-specific, state-specific and performance grants -- reflects what underlying approach to fiscal federalism?
options: A layered approach that combines objective, needs- and equity-based formula devolution with targeted, need- or performance-specific grants to address gaps the formula alone cannot
A purely formula-only approach with no role for any discretionary or targeted grants
A system where all funds are distributed equally to every State regardless of any criteria
A system that eliminates any distinction between States and local governments
questions.explanation: The Commission's overall design layers a broad, criteria-based devolution formula with targeted grants addressing specific gaps (deficits, disasters, sectors, local bodies, performance) -- a deliberately layered, not purely formulaic, not equal-for-all, and not local-government-blind approach to fiscal federalism.

questions.locator: 2023 paper's item on Fifteenth Finance Commission criteria
questions.source_excerpt: The paper tests whether candidates know that the Fifteenth Finance Commission used additional criteria -- such as demographic performance, forest and ecology, and tax and fiscal effort -- beyond population, area, and income distance for horizontal tax devolution.
questions.question: One 2023 prelims question asks how many criteria, besides population, area, and income distance, the Fifteenth Finance Commission used for horizontal tax devolution among States. Which of the following is one of those additional criteria?
options: Forest and ecology
Literacy rate
Number of Lok Sabha seats
State's coastline length
questions.explanation: Forest and ecology is one of the additional horizontal devolution criteria used by the Fifteenth Finance Commission (alongside demographic performance and tax and fiscal effort), beyond population, area, and income distance. Literacy rate, Lok Sabha seat count, and coastline length are not among the Commission's devolution criteria.

questions.locator: 2023 paper's item on the G20
questions.source_excerpt: The paper tests the original institutional purpose of the G20: a platform for Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors.
questions.question: The 2023 paper tests the original institutional purpose of the G20. As a fiscal/economic coordination body, the G20 initially brought together which set of officials?
options: Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors
Defence Ministers and military chiefs
Trade union leaders
Chief Justices of member countries
questions.explanation: The G20 was originally founded as a forum for Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors of major economies to discuss international financial stability and economic coordination -- not defence officials, labour leaders, or judiciary heads.

questions.locator: 2023 paper's item on Digital Public Infrastructure as a G20 priority
questions.source_excerpt: The paper tests awareness of India's G20 priorities, including Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI).
questions.question: The 2023 paper also tests awareness of India's G20 priorities, including 'Digital Public Infrastructure' (DPI). In the context of public finance and governance, what does DPI broadly refer to?
options: Shared, foundational digital systems (such as digital identity and payments platforms) that governments and economies build upon to deliver services and enable financial inclusion at scale
A single private company's proprietary banking software
A physical road and bridge construction programme
A defence procurement database
questions.explanation: Digital Public Infrastructure refers to foundational, often open, digital systems -- like digital identity and payment rails -- that both government and private actors can build services on top of, expanding financial inclusion and service delivery; it is not a single company's private software, physical infrastructure, or a defence system.

questions.locator: 2023 paper's item on the Production-Linked Incentive scheme
questions.source_excerpt: The paper tests awareness of the Production-Linked Incentive scheme as a conditional, performance-linked government expenditure instrument.
questions.question: From a public-finance perspective, the Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme represents which kind of government expenditure instrument?
options: A performance-linked subsidy/incentive expenditure, disbursed based on companies achieving incremental production or sales targets, rather than an unconditional grant
A one-time capital grant with no performance conditions attached
A reduction in the corporate tax rate applicable to all companies uniformly
A loan guarantee scheme with no incentive-linked disbursement
questions.explanation: PLI is structured as conditional, performance-linked expenditure -- funds are disbursed only as companies hit incremental production/sales milestones -- distinguishing it from an unconditional one-time grant, a uniform tax-rate cut, or a loan-guarantee instrument.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's description of the programme's broad strategy
questions.source_excerpt: The broad strategy of the Aspirational Districts Programme includes: Convergence - between Central and State Schemes; Collaboration - between Centre, State, District Administration, Development Partners and Citizens; Competition - between Districts.
questions.question: The Aspirational Districts Programme's broad delivery strategy rests on three pillars. Which set correctly names them?
options: Convergence, Collaboration, Competition
Centralisation, Delegation, Automation
Planning, Budgeting, Auditing
Recruitment, Training, Promotion
questions.explanation: The programme's official strategy names Convergence (between Central and State schemes), Collaboration (across Centre, State, district administration, partners, and citizens) and Competition (between districts) as its three pillars -- the other option sets are unrelated management terms.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's section on institutional arrangement
questions.source_excerpt: For each district, a central Prabhari officer of the rank of Additional Secretary/Joint Secretary has been nominated.
questions.question: For each Aspirational District, a central 'Prabhari officer' of Additional Secretary/Joint Secretary rank is nominated. What programme-management function does this role serve?
options: It gives each district a dedicated, senior central-government point of contact/champion to help drive and coordinate its transformation
It transfers full administrative control of the district away from the State government
It is a ceremonial title with no operational responsibility
It duplicates the role of the elected Member of Parliament for that district
questions.explanation: The Prabhari officer gives each district a senior, named central-government champion to help coordinate and drive progress -- it does not strip the State government of administrative control, is not merely ceremonial, and is distinct from an elected MP's role.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's section on institutional arrangement
questions.source_excerpt: An Empowered Committee under the convener-ship of CEO, NITI Aayog has been notified to ensure convergence in schemes and address specific issues brought out by Prabhari officers.
questions.question: An Empowered Committee, convened by the CEO of NITI Aayog, was set up under the Aspirational Districts Programme. What is this committee's primary role?
options: Ensuring convergence between different government schemes and resolving specific issues raised by Prabhari officers
Directly disbursing salaries to district-level government staff
Conducting judicial review of state government decisions
Selecting which political party governs a given district
questions.explanation: The Empowered Committee exists to ensure scheme convergence and resolve issues flagged by Prabhari officers -- a coordination and problem-resolution function, not payroll administration, judicial review, or any role in district-level politics.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's section on the Champions of Change dashboard
questions.source_excerpt: Champions of Change (CoC) is the backbone of the Aspirational Districts Programme. The new CoC digital platform facilitates advanced data analytics, digitised project management workflow, and machine-learning capabilities.
questions.question: The 'Champions of Change' digital platform is described as the backbone of the Aspirational Districts Programme, supporting data analytics and digitised project management workflows. What programme-management function does this platform primarily serve?
options: It provides a real-time, data-driven monitoring and project-management backbone to track each district's progress
It functions solely as a public grievance redress portal, unrelated to programme progress
It replaces the need for any Prabhari officer or Empowered Committee
It is used exclusively for internal staff recruitment
questions.explanation: Champions of Change is built as a data-analytics and project-management platform to track district progress in real time -- it is not a grievance portal, does not replace the human coordination roles, and is not a recruitment tool.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's section on Delta ranking
questions.source_excerpt: This programme focuses on the strength of each district, measuring progress by ranking districts on a monthly basis. The ranking is based on the incremental progress made across 49 Key Performance Indicators.
questions.question: Rather than ranking districts only once against a fixed baseline, the programme also produces a monthly 'Delta ranking' based on incremental progress on 49 KPIs. Why does adding this incremental ranking matter for programme management, compared to a single static baseline ranking alone?
options: It lets even a historically low-performing district be recognised for the pace of its recent improvement, creating an ongoing incentive to keep improving rather than being permanently judged only against its starting position
It replaces the need for any baseline measurement at all
It ranks districts only once every five years instead of monthly
It measures each district's improvement relative to districts in other countries
questions.explanation: A monthly incremental (delta) ranking rewards recent progress regardless of a district's starting point, sustaining motivation for continuous improvement -- it complements rather than replaces the baseline, is explicitly monthly, and compares districts within India, not internationally.

questions.locator: PIB backgrounder's table of theme weights and data-points
questions.source_excerpt: Health & Nutrition 30% (31 data-points); Education 30% (14); Agriculture & Water Resources 20% (12); Financial Inclusion 5% (6); Skill Development 5% (10); Basic Infrastructure 10% (8). Total 100% (81 data-points).
questions.question: The programme's composite ranking weights Health & Nutrition and Education at 30% each, Agriculture & Water Resources at 20%, and Financial Inclusion, Skill Development, and Basic Infrastructure at smaller shares. As a programme-management choice, what does this weighting scheme achieve?
options: It signals which thematic areas are treated as the highest programme priorities for districts to focus scarce implementation effort and resources on
It guarantees every theme receives an identical share of district-level budgets
It has no bearing on how districts prioritise their own action plans
It is recalculated separately for every individual district based on local preference
questions.explanation: Assigning higher weights to Health & Nutrition and Education signals that these are the programme's top priorities, guiding districts on where to focus limited implementation effort -- the weighting is a common national scheme, not identical budget shares, and not irrelevant to district planning.

questions.locator: Handbook's description of the target audience -- Ministries, Departments and Organisations (MDOs)
questions.source_excerpt: The handbook is addressed to Ministries, Departments and Organisations (MDOs) responsible for planning and delivering capacity-building interventions for their personnel.
questions.question: The Capacity Building Commission's handbook on performance measurement is addressed to 'MDOs.' In the Mission Karmayogi context, what does MDO refer to?
options: Ministries, Departments and Organisations
Municipal Development Officers only
Medical Data Officers
Multilateral Development Organisations (international agencies)
questions.explanation: In the Mission Karmayogi/Capacity Building Commission framework, MDO stands for Ministries, Departments and Organisations -- the government entities responsible for planning and delivering capacity-building for their own staff -- not municipal or medical officers, and not international multilateral bodies.

questions.locator: Handbook's stated rationale
questions.source_excerpt: Capacity-building efforts may improve individual knowledge and skills, but without a clear measurement approach, MDOs cannot tell whether this translates into improved on-the-job performance or service delivery.
questions.question: What core programme-management gap does the Capacity Building Commission's handbook aim to address for MDOs running capacity-building interventions?
options: The absence of a clear approach for measuring whether capacity-building efforts actually translate into improved performance and service delivery, not just completed training
A shortage of physical classroom space for government training
The complete absence of any training programmes for civil servants
A legal ban on evaluating civil servants' performance
questions.explanation: The handbook's rationale is that MDOs often lack a clear framework for measuring whether training-based capacity building actually improves on-the-job performance and service delivery -- not that classroom space is lacking, that training programmes are absent, or that a legal prohibition exists on evaluating performance.

questions.locator: Handbook's distinction between training completion and performance improvement
questions.source_excerpt: The handbook distinguishes between merely tracking training completion and assessing actual performance improvement.
questions.question: The handbook distinguishes between merely tracking training completion and assessing actual performance improvement. If an MDO only reports 'X employees completed Y training hours,' which type of measure is it reporting?
options: An output measure, not necessarily evidence of improved outcomes
A pure impact/outcome measure of performance change
A measure of citizen satisfaction with service delivery
A financial audit measure of budget utilisation
questions.explanation: Training completion counts (employees trained, hours logged) are output measures -- they show activity happened, but do not by themselves demonstrate that on-the-job performance or service delivery improved, which is the outcome the handbook pushes MDOs to measure separately.

questions.locator: Handbook's description of the measurement approach's steps
questions.source_excerpt: The approach involves defining clear Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) tied to the intended capacity-building outcomes before tracking progress against them.
questions.question: According to the handbook's performance-measurement approach, what needs to happen before an MDO can meaningfully track whether a capacity-building intervention is working?
options: Clear Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) linked to the intended outcomes must be defined first
All employees must first complete every available training course, regardless of relevance
The MDO must first eliminate its training budget entirely
A parliamentary committee must approve every individual employee's training record
questions.explanation: The handbook's approach starts with defining clear, outcome-linked KPIs -- without that step, later monitoring has nothing meaningful to track against. It does not require exhaustive training completion, budget elimination, or parliamentary sign-off on individual records.

questions.locator: Handbook's description of continuous, dashboard-based monitoring
questions.source_excerpt: The approach envisages continuous, real-time tracking of capacity-building KPIs through a dashboard, rather than periodic, ad hoc reviews.
questions.question: The handbook's approach favours continuous, dashboard-based tracking of capacity-building KPIs. What programme-management advantage does continuous monitoring offer over infrequent, ad hoc reviews?
options: It surfaces performance gaps sooner, allowing MDOs to make timely course corrections rather than discovering problems only much later
It removes any need for MDOs to define KPIs in the first place
It eliminates the value of any human judgment in interpreting the data
It only works for MDOs with fewer than ten employees
questions.explanation: Continuous monitoring surfaces issues early enough for timely correction, unlike infrequent ad hoc reviews that may catch problems only long after they have compounded -- it still requires clearly defined KPIs, does not eliminate human interpretation, and is not limited by organisation size.

questions.locator: Handbook's overall purpose as a shared methodology for MDOs
questions.source_excerpt: The Capacity Building Commission's handbook provides MDOs with a structured, common methodology for measuring capacity-building performance.
questions.question: By providing MDOs with a structured methodology for measuring capacity-building performance, the Capacity Building Commission's handbook is itself an example of what broader programme-management principle?
options: Building standardised organisational capability/tools so that many different implementing units can apply a consistent measurement approach, rather than each one improvising its own method
Centralising all capacity-building delivery into a single ministry, eliminating MDOs' role entirely
Replacing the need for MDOs to have any monitoring function of their own
Applying only to private-sector companies, not government MDOs
questions.explanation: A shared handbook/methodology standardises how many different MDOs measure performance, avoiding fragmented, inconsistent approaches -- it does not centralise delivery into one ministry, does not remove MDOs' own monitoring responsibility, and is meant for government MDOs, not private companies.

questions.locator: Guideline's section on Service Delivery Capability
questions.source_excerpt: Service Delivery Capability includes the standard operating procedures, staff orientation/training, and infrastructure needed to meet the charter's commitments.
questions.question: From a programme (implementation) management perspective, why does Sevottam treat 'Service Delivery Capability' as a distinct component from the Citizen's Charter itself, rather than assuming a published charter is sufficient?
options: Because publishing service standards is not the same as having the trained staff, processes, and systems in place to actually deliver on them -- capability has to be built and managed separately
Because Service Delivery Capability refers only to the physical size of a department's office building
Because the Citizen's Charter and Service Delivery Capability must always be published as one identical document
Because capability-building is entirely outside any government department's control
questions.explanation: Sevottam separates capability from the charter because promising standards on paper does not guarantee an organisation can deliver them -- capability (staff, SOPs, systems) has to be deliberately built and managed as its own implementation workstream, not reduced to office size, merged into one document, or treated as beyond a department's control.

questions.locator: Guideline's discussion of the underlying service-standard-setting cycle
questions.source_excerpt: The underlying approach requires organisations to define services and clients, set standards, build capability, perform, monitor, evaluate independently, and improve.
questions.question: Viewed as a programme-delivery cycle -- define, set standards, build capability, perform, monitor, evaluate, improve -- what happens if an organisation skips the 'monitor performance' step but still claims to be improving continuously?
options: Its claimed 'continuous improvement' would lack any real evidence base, since improvement decisions are supposed to be driven by what monitoring reveals
Nothing changes, since monitoring has no connection to the improvement step
The organisation would automatically fail to define its services or clients
It would only affect grievance redress and nothing else in service delivery
questions.explanation: In the model's cyclical logic, 'improvement' is supposed to be informed by what monitoring and evaluation reveal about actual performance -- skipping monitoring removes the evidence base that improvement claims should rest on. It does not retroactively undo an earlier step, and it affects the whole cycle's credibility, not just grievance redress.

questions.locator: Guideline's section on grievance redress as a feedback channel
questions.source_excerpt: A grievance redress mechanism receives, records, investigates, and addresses complaints, revealing recurring service delivery issues.
questions.question: In programme management terms, why is a formal grievance redress mechanism useful to the people running a public-service delivery programme, beyond simply satisfying individual complainants?
options: It surfaces recurring, systemic delivery problems that programme managers might not otherwise detect, functioning as an early-warning/feedback channel
It has no informational value to programme managers -- its only purpose is closing individual complaints
It is purely a legal formality with no link to improving service delivery
It replaces the need for any performance monitoring of the programme
questions.explanation: Beyond resolving individual complaints, a well-run grievance mechanism reveals recurring or systemic problems that feed back into programme management as an early-warning signal -- it is not purely a legal formality, does have real informational value for managers, and complements rather than replaces performance monitoring.

questions.locator: Guideline's discussion of Citizen's Charter service standards and timelines
questions.source_excerpt: A Citizen's Charter states measurable service standards, including timelines a department commits to for delivering a given service.
questions.question: A department's Citizen's Charter commits to specific service timelines (e.g. issuing a certificate within a stated number of days). How does publishing such a timeline function as a programme-management tool, not just a citizen-facing promise?
options: It creates an internal benchmark that the department's own delivery process must be planned and staffed to meet, making the promise a management target as well as a public commitment
It has no effect on how the department internally plans its workflow
It is legally unenforceable and therefore carries no management significance
It only applies to departments with fewer than five employees
questions.explanation: A published timeline becomes an internal delivery benchmark that shapes staffing and process planning, not merely an external-facing promise disconnected from internal management -- and it applies regardless of department size.

questions.locator: Guideline's discussion of Sevottam compliance assessment/certification
questions.source_excerpt: Departments can be assessed and certified as Sevottam compliant based on adherence to its three components.
questions.question: Departments can be assessed and certified as 'Sevottam compliant' based on adherence to its three components. What programme-management role does this compliance certification play?
options: It functions as an external quality-assurance checkpoint, verifying that a department's charter, grievance mechanism, and delivery capability actually meet the model's standards, rather than relying only on the department's own self-assessment
It automatically increases a department's budget allocation with no further review
It replaces the need for the department to have a Citizen's Charter at all
It applies only to central government departments, never to any assessment process for states
questions.explanation: Compliance certification provides an external quality-assurance checkpoint against the Sevottam standards, rather than leaving assessment purely to internal self-reporting -- it does not itself change budget allocations, does not remove the need for a charter, and the framework's use is not confined to a single level of government.

questions.locator: Handbook's opening rationale
questions.source_excerpt: The handbook identifies the absence of a clear, consistent system to measure how capacity-building interventions actually affect on-the-job performance and service delivery.
questions.question: What foundational monitoring-and-evaluation gap does the Capacity Building Commission's handbook identify regarding government capacity-building efforts before it proposes its measurement approach?
options: The absence of a clear, consistent system to measure how capacity-building interventions actually affect on-the-job performance and service delivery
A complete absence of any capacity-building or training activity across government
A shortage of physical training venues nationwide
A prohibition on collecting any employee performance data
questions.explanation: The handbook's starting premise is that while capacity-building activity exists, there had been no clear system for measuring its actual effect on performance and service delivery -- not that training itself was absent, that venues were lacking, or that performance data collection was prohibited.

questions.locator: Handbook's distinction between output and outcome indicators
questions.source_excerpt: The handbook distinguishes tracking training completion (an output) from assessing actual performance improvement (an outcome).
questions.question: For monitoring and evaluation purposes, why is it important for an MDO to track outcome indicators (e.g. observed improvement in a specific job function) separately from output indicators (e.g. training hours completed)?
options: Because a high output number (lots of training delivered) does not guarantee the outcome (actual performance improvement) occurred, and only outcome tracking can confirm whether the intervention worked
Because output and outcome indicators always move in perfect lockstep, so tracking either one is redundant
Because outcome indicators are easier and faster to collect than output indicators
Because output indicators are irrelevant to any M&E framework and should never be collected
questions.explanation: Outputs and outcomes can diverge -- lots of training delivered does not guarantee it changed actual performance -- so a sound M&E design tracks both, using outcome data to judge whether the intervention truly worked. Outcome data is typically harder, not easier, to collect than output counts, and outputs remain useful as an intermediate indicator, not an irrelevant one.

questions.locator: Handbook's description of the measurement approach's first step
questions.source_excerpt: The approach starts with defining Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) before establishing a baseline and target.
questions.question: In designing a monitoring framework for a capacity-building programme, the handbook's approach starts with defining Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). Why must this happen before setting any baseline or target?
options: Because a baseline and target are only meaningful once you know exactly what indicator you are measuring against them
Because KPIs can be defined at any point, even after the programme has ended, with no effect on the evaluation
Because targets should always be set before deciding what to measure
Because baselines are unnecessary once KPIs exist
questions.explanation: A baseline and a target both need a defined indicator to be measured against -- defining KPIs first is a logical prerequisite, not something that can be deferred to the end of a programme, and baselines remain necessary even once KPIs are defined, to know the starting point for measuring change.

questions.locator: Handbook's description of real-time, dashboard-based tracking
