questions.source_excerpt: The approach favours real-time monitoring of capacity-building KPIs through a dashboard.
questions.question: The handbook's approach favours real-time monitoring of capacity-building KPIs through a dashboard. In monitoring-and-evaluation terms, what is the primary value of 'real-time' rather than only end-of-cycle reporting?
options: It creates a continuous learning loop, letting MDOs spot underperforming indicators and adjust while the programme is still running, rather than only learning about problems after it has ended
It removes any need to ever conduct an end-of-cycle evaluation
It is valuable only for financial audits, not for capacity-building programmes
It means data only needs to be collected once a year
questions.explanation: Real-time dashboards enable a continuous learning loop -- catching underperformance while there is still time to act -- rather than discovering issues only in a final end-of-cycle report; it complements rather than replaces periodic evaluation, applies to programme monitoring broadly, and implies frequent, not once-yearly, data collection.

questions.locator: Handbook's description of data-driven goal setting
questions.source_excerpt: The approach describes data-driven goal setting as part of continuous performance analysis.
questions.question: The handbook describes 'data-driven goal setting' as part of its approach. What does this most likely mean in an M&E context, as opposed to setting targets once and never revisiting them?
options: Targets are set and periodically revised based on what the monitoring data shows about actual progress, rather than being fixed permanently at the outset
Targets are chosen entirely at random, independent of any data
Only one target is ever set for the lifetime of any programme, with no revision
Data is collected but deliberately never used to inform any targets
questions.explanation: Data-driven goal setting implies targets are informed and periodically revised based on actual monitoring data, rather than fixed once at the start and never revisited -- the opposite of random target-setting or data collection that is never actually used.

questions.locator: Handbook's overall purpose as a shared measurement methodology
questions.source_excerpt: The Capacity Building Commission issued a common performance-measurement handbook for MDOs rather than leaving each to design its own.
questions.question: Why does it matter, from an M&E systems-design standpoint, that the Capacity Building Commission issued a dedicated handbook on performance measurement specifically for MDOs, rather than leaving each MDO to invent its own approach?
options: A shared methodology improves comparability and quality of M&E practice across many different government organisations, instead of leaving quality dependent on each MDO's own ad hoc effort
It guarantees that every MDO will report identical numerical results regardless of actual performance
It removes the need for any MDO to collect its own data going forward
It applies only to one specific ministry and no others
questions.explanation: A common, shared measurement methodology raises the floor and improves comparability of M&E practice across many MDOs, rather than leaving quality dependent on each organisation's own improvised approach -- it does not force identical results irrespective of performance, does not eliminate MDOs' own data collection, and is meant to apply broadly across MDOs.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on designing and monitoring policy frameworks
questions.source_excerpt: To design strategic and long term policy and programme frameworks and initiatives, and monitor their progress and their efficacy.
questions.question: The resolution's objective to 'design strategic and long term policy and programme frameworks... and monitor their progress and their efficacy' assigns NITI Aayog what kind of ongoing role, beyond one-time policy design?
options: A continuing monitoring-and-evaluation role, tracking whether policies and programmes are actually working over time
A role limited strictly to drafting documents, with no tracking of implementation afterward
A role that ends the moment a policy framework is approved
A purely ceremonial role with no connection to actual programme data
questions.explanation: By explicitly pairing 'design' with a duty to 'monitor progress and efficacy,' the resolution assigns an ongoing M&E function, not a one-time drafting role that stops once a document is approved, and not a ceremonial function disconnected from real programme performance.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on monitoring/evaluation and resource identification
questions.source_excerpt: To actively monitor and evaluate the implementation of programmes and initiatives, including the identification of the needed resources so as to strengthen the probability of success and scope of delivery.
questions.question: This objective links monitoring and evaluation directly to 'identification of the needed resources so as to strengthen the probability of success.' What does this reveal about how the resolution expects M&E findings to be used?
options: M&E findings are expected to feed forward into practical decisions about resourcing, so problems identified through monitoring translate into corrective action, not just a report
M&E findings are meant to be filed away with no further action taken
M&E is meant only to justify shutting down every underperforming programme immediately, with no resourcing adjustments considered
M&E has no connection at all to how much funding or staffing a programme receives
questions.explanation: Explicitly linking M&E to identifying 'needed resources' shows the resolution expects monitoring findings to feed forward into resourcing decisions to improve delivery -- not to be filed away unused, not to trigger automatic programme termination, and clearly connected to funding/staffing decisions.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on village-level plan aggregation
questions.source_excerpt: To develop mechanisms to formulate credible plans at the village level and aggregate these progressively at higher levels of government.
questions.question: The resolution calls for credible plans to be formulated at the village level and then aggregated progressively upward. From a monitoring-and-evaluation design standpoint, why does starting data/plans at the most local level support more credible higher-level indicators?
options: Because indicators built up from accurate, locally grounded information are less likely to be distorted than figures imposed top-down without local verification
Because village-level data is always less accurate than data estimated at the national level
Because aggregation upward has no bearing on the credibility of any resulting indicator
Because this approach only applies to financial indicators, not to any other kind of development indicator
questions.explanation: Grounding indicators in locally verified, bottom-up information tends to produce more credible aggregated figures than numbers imposed from the top without local grounding -- the opposite of assuming local data is always less accurate, and the aggregation logic is described generally for development plans, not restricted to financial indicators.

questions.locator: Resolution's objective on the resource centre
questions.source_excerpt: To provide a resource centre for research on good governance and best practices in sustainable and equitable development as well as help their dissemination to stake-holders.
questions.question: NITI Aayog's role as a 'resource centre' for research and best practices, disseminated to stakeholders, supports which specific monitoring-and-evaluation function across states?
options: Spreading effective evaluation approaches and lessons learned from one state or programme so that others can adopt or adapt them, rather than every state having to independently discover the same lessons
Preventing any state from developing its own evaluation capacity
Restricting evaluation findings so that only the Union government ever sees them
Replacing the need for any state to conduct its own monitoring
questions.explanation: A resource centre that shares best practices helps spread effective evaluation lessons across states, avoiding duplicated learning -- it does not prevent states from building their own capacity, does not restrict findings to the Union government alone, and does not substitute for each state doing its own monitoring.

questions.locator: Resolution's overall design as an advisory, non-allocative body
questions.source_excerpt: NITI Aayog was designed as an advisory think tank without the Planning Commission's power to allocate plan funds to States.
questions.question: Because NITI Aayog, unlike the Planning Commission, does not directly control plan-fund allocations to states, how does the resolution's monitoring-and-evaluation mandate become especially important to its ability to influence state performance?
options: Without financial leverage, credible monitoring and evaluation evidence becomes one of NITI Aayog's main tools for persuading states and driving improved performance through comparison, feedback, and reputational incentives
Monitoring and evaluation become irrelevant once financial leverage is removed
The resolution compensates for the lack of financial control by granting NITI Aayog direct disciplinary power over state officials
States are legally compelled to follow every NITI Aayog recommendation regardless of any evidence
questions.explanation: With no direct control over plan funds, NITI Aayog leans more heavily on the credibility of its monitoring and evaluation work -- using evidence, comparison, and reputational/peer incentives -- to influence states, rather than compulsion; it holds no direct disciplinary power over state officials and state compliance is not legally compelled.

questions.locator: Resolution's shift from Five-Year-Plan review cycles to continuous engagement
questions.source_excerpt: The resolution replaces the Planning Commission's Five-Year Plan model with continuous, structured engagement and ongoing identification of resource needs.
questions.question: The Planning Commission's Five-Year Plans were built around fixed multi-year targets reviewed at set intervals. How does the monitoring-and-evaluation orientation implied by NITI Aayog's resolution objectives (continuous structured engagement, real-time identification of resource needs) differ from that older model?
options: It leans toward more continuous, ongoing tracking and course-correction rather than waiting for fixed, multi-year review points
There is no meaningful difference -- both models are described in the resolution as identical
NITI Aayog's approach abandons target-setting of any kind
The resolution mandates reviews only once every five years, exactly matching the old Plan cycle
questions.explanation: The resolution's objectives (continuous structured support, ongoing identification of resource needs) point toward a more continuous monitoring orientation than the older fixed multi-year Five-Year-Plan review cycle -- it does not abandon target-related thinking altogether, is not identical to the old model, and is not tied to a rigid five-year review interval.

questions.locator: Document's institutional background
questions.source_excerpt: The PMGSY evaluation was conducted by what later became the Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office (DMEO), formed in 2015 by merging the erstwhile Programme Evaluation Organisation and Independent Evaluation Office, as an attached office of NITI Aayog.
questions.question: The PMGSY evaluation was conducted by what later became the Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office (DMEO). How was DMEO formed?
options: By merging the earlier Programme Evaluation Organisation and Independent Evaluation Office into a single attached office of NITI Aayog
By splitting NITI Aayog into two separate, unrelated bodies
As a private-sector consultancy hired on a one-time basis
As a new wing of the Union Ministry of Finance with no link to NITI Aayog
questions.explanation: DMEO was created in 2015 by merging the erstwhile Programme Evaluation Organisation and the Independent Evaluation Office into a single attached office under NITI Aayog -- not by splitting NITI Aayog, and not as a private consultancy or Finance Ministry wing.

questions.locator: Document's title -- 'A Quick Concurrent Evaluation of PMGSY'
questions.source_excerpt: The report's title describes it as a quick concurrent evaluation, conducted while PMGSY implementation was ongoing.
questions.question: The report is titled 'A Quick Concurrent Evaluation of PMGSY.' What does labelling an evaluation 'concurrent' indicate about its timing, in monitoring-and-evaluation terms?
options: It was conducted while the programme was still ongoing/being implemented, rather than only after it had fully concluded
It was conducted only after the scheme had been permanently shut down
It refers to two entirely unrelated schemes being evaluated together
It means the evaluation used no data at all, only expert opinion
questions.explanation: 'Concurrent' evaluation means the assessment happens alongside ongoing implementation, not only after a programme ends (that would be an 'ex-post' evaluation) -- it does not refer to evaluating unrelated schemes together, nor does it imply an absence of data.

questions.locator: Document's rationale for evaluating PMGSY while implementation is ongoing
questions.source_excerpt: A concurrent evaluation allows findings to feed back into an ongoing programme, unlike an evaluation conducted only after completion.
questions.question: What is the main monitoring-and-evaluation advantage of a 'concurrent' evaluation of an ongoing scheme like PMGSY, compared to waiting until the scheme is fully complete to evaluate it?
options: Findings can feed back into the programme while it is still running, allowing implementers to make mid-course corrections rather than only learning lessons after it is too late to act
It produces identical findings to a post-completion evaluation, so the timing makes no practical difference
It removes the need to ever conduct a follow-up evaluation later
It can only be conducted using satellite imagery, with no field or administrative data
questions.explanation: The core value of concurrent evaluation is enabling mid-course correction while the programme is still active -- timing does make a practical difference compared to waiting until completion, it does not preclude later follow-up evaluations, and it is not restricted to any single data-collection method.

questions.locator: PMGSY's well-known implementation tracking system
questions.source_excerpt: PMGSY implementation is tracked through the Online Management, Monitoring and Accounting System (OMMAS), a management information system used to track project status and expenditure.
questions.question: PMGSY's implementation has long been tracked through an online system known as OMMAS. What is OMMAS primarily used for?
options: Tracking project status, physical progress, and expenditure of PMGSY road works through a management information system
Issuing driving licences to residents of connected habitations
Selecting which state gets to host the scheme's annual conference
Auditing unrelated urban housing schemes
questions.explanation: OMMAS (Online Management, Monitoring and Accounting System) is PMGSY's management information system for tracking the physical and financial progress of road works -- unrelated to driving licences, hosting conferences, or auditing other, unrelated urban schemes.

questions.locator: Document's discussion of road quality and maintenance as evaluation indicators
questions.source_excerpt: The evaluation examines road quality/durability and post-construction maintenance arrangements as part of assessing PMGSY's delivery.
questions.question: A monitoring-and-evaluation exercise for a rural road connectivity scheme like PMGSY needs to look beyond simply 'how many kilometres were built.' Why is tracking road quality and post-construction maintenance arrangements also an important indicator?
options: Because a road that deteriorates quickly without proper maintenance may stop delivering reliable connectivity soon after construction, undermining the scheme's actual purpose even though the kilometre-built target was met
Because road quality has no bearing on whether a habitation stays connected over time
Because kilometres built is the only indicator that matters for any road scheme
Because maintenance is entirely the responsibility of individual villagers, with no institutional tracking needed
questions.explanation: Quality and maintenance determine whether connectivity, once achieved, actually lasts -- a road that is built but not maintained can quickly become unusable, meaning the raw 'kilometres constructed' output can overstate real, sustained connectivity. Maintenance is typically an institutional responsibility, not left solely to villagers.

questions.locator: Document's discussion of connectivity and usage outcomes
questions.source_excerpt: The evaluation assesses usage-based outcomes -- such as access to markets, schools, and health facilities -- beyond the count of roads constructed.
questions.question: Beyond counting roads constructed, an evaluation of PMGSY's actual effect would also look at usage-based outcome indicators, such as whether connected habitations show improved access to markets, schools, or health facilities. Why is this outcome-level check necessary in addition to the output count?
options: Because building a road does not automatically guarantee it translates into meaningfully improved access and use by the local population -- that has to be separately verified
Because roads are, by definition, never actually used once constructed
Because output counts (kilometres built) are always a perfect substitute for outcome data
Because outcome-level checks are legally prohibited under PMGSY's evaluation framework
questions.explanation: A constructed road is an output; whether it actually improves people's access to markets, schools, or health facilities is a separate outcome question that needs its own verification -- output counts are not automatically equivalent to outcomes, and there is no such prohibition on outcome-level assessment.

questions.locator: Document's methodology note on the 'quick concurrent' evaluation design
questions.source_excerpt: A quick concurrent evaluation trades some methodological depth for speed, providing early evidence while the programme is still being implemented.
questions.question: How does a 'quick concurrent evaluation' of PMGSY, conducted while the scheme is still being implemented, typically differ in rigour from a full ex-post impact evaluation conducted years after roads are built?
options: It trades some methodological rigour and long-run outcome data for speed, providing early, directional evidence rather than definitive proof of long-term impact
It is always more methodologically rigorous than any later ex-post evaluation
There is no meaningful difference between the two types of evaluation
It focuses exclusively on outcomes occurring decades after implementation
questions.explanation: A quick, concurrent evaluation prioritises speed and early feedback over the years of follow-up data and rigorous comparison-group designs a full ex-post impact evaluation can use -- it typically offers directional, not definitive, evidence, is not inherently more rigorous, and differs clearly from a later evaluation rather than being identical to it.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using PMGSY
questions.source_excerpt: Impact evaluation of a road connectivity scheme requires estimating what would have happened to a village without the road -- the counterfactual.
questions.question: In evaluating PMGSY's impact on a village's economic activity, evaluators need to estimate the 'counterfactual' -- what would have happened without the road. Why is the counterfactual central to impact evaluation, as opposed to simple monitoring?
options: Because impact is defined as the difference between what actually happened with the intervention and what would have happened without it, not simply what happened after the intervention
Because the counterfactual is simply the exact same data as what was observed after the road was built
Because monitoring and impact evaluation are identical activities requiring no separate counterfactual concept
Because a counterfactual only matters for evaluating urban infrastructure, not rural roads
questions.explanation: Impact is fundamentally a comparison between the observed outcome and the counterfactual (what would have happened anyway) -- without an estimate of that counterfactual, one cannot distinguish the road's actual effect from other changes happening regardless. It is not the same as post-intervention data, and this need for a counterfactual is precisely what distinguishes impact evaluation from simple monitoring.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using PMGSY
questions.source_excerpt: A simple before-after comparison of a village's outcomes cannot rule out other concurrent changes as the true cause.
questions.question: Suppose an evaluator compares a village's income levels before and after PMGSY connects it to a market town, and attributes the entire income increase to the new road. What is the key methodological problem with this simple before-after comparison?
options: It cannot rule out that other factors occurring over the same period (e.g. a good monsoon, other government schemes, general economic growth) also contributed to or fully explain the income change
Before-after comparisons are always the single most rigorous method available for any impact evaluation
There is no methodological problem, since only PMGSY could possibly affect village income
The problem only arises if the road happens to be paved rather than unpaved
questions.explanation: A simple before-after comparison confounds the road's effect with any other changes happening over the same period -- weather, other schemes, broader economic trends -- so it cannot cleanly isolate PMGSY's contribution. It is not the most rigorous available method precisely for this reason, other factors clearly could affect income, and the issue has nothing to do with pavement type.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using PMGSY's eligibility rules
questions.source_excerpt: PMGSY has historically prioritised connectivity for habitations above a fixed population threshold, differing by area category.
questions.question: PMGSY has historically prioritised connectivity for habitations above a fixed population threshold. In principle, how could this rule-based cutoff be used to support a more credible impact evaluation design, compared to simply comparing any connected village to any unconnected one?
options: By comparing habitations just above and just below the population cutoff, which are likely to be otherwise similar, isolating the road's effect from broader differences between very large and very small habitations
By ensuring that every habitation in the country was connected at exactly the same time, eliminating any need for comparison
By guaranteeing that population size has no relationship to which habitations get connected first
By making it impossible to ever construct a comparison group
questions.explanation: Habitations just above and just below a population cutoff tend to be otherwise similar, so comparing them approximates a natural experiment that better isolates the road's effect from confounding differences -- unlike comparing very differently sized villages at large. Connectivity was explicitly staggered by criteria like population, not universally simultaneous, and the cutoff is exactly what makes a comparison group possible.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using PMGSY
questions.source_excerpt: Kilometres of road constructed is an output; increased household income from better market access would be a downstream impact.
questions.question: For PMGSY, 'kilometres of all-weather road constructed' is an output, while 'increased household income from better market access' would be a downstream impact. Why is this distinction important when designing an impact evaluation?
options: Because achieving the output does not automatically prove the intended downstream impact occurred -- that requires its own separate evidence and causal analysis
Because outputs and impacts are simply two different names for exactly the same measurement
Because only outputs can ever be reliably measured, while impacts can never be measured at all
Because impact evaluations should only ever look at outputs, never at downstream effects
questions.explanation: Outputs (roads built) and impacts (income, welfare changes) are conceptually distinct -- completing the output doesn't guarantee the hoped-for downstream impact materialised, so impact evaluation must gather separate evidence on the downstream outcome, not just confirm the output was delivered.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using PMGSY's quick-evaluation timing
questions.source_excerpt: Downstream impacts of connectivity, such as changes in school enrolment or household income, typically take years to materialise and stabilise.
questions.question: Why might a 'quick' evaluation of PMGSY be well-suited to assessing outputs (roads completed, quality) but poorly suited to detecting the programme's full downstream impact (e.g. long-run changes in school enrollment or household income)?
options: Because many downstream impacts take years to materialise and stabilise, so a quick evaluation conducted soon after construction may be too early to capture them reliably
Because downstream impacts always appear before the road itself is even completed
Because outputs, unlike impacts, cannot be assessed quickly under any evaluation design
Because there is no realistic time lag between building a road and any resulting change in household income
questions.explanation: Downstream impacts like income or enrollment changes often take years to show up and stabilise, so an evaluation conducted soon after construction risks measuring too early -- outputs like completed kilometres, by contrast, are observable almost immediately. Impacts do not precede the intervention that causes them, and there typically is a meaningful time lag to account for.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using overlapping rural schemes
questions.source_excerpt: Villages receiving PMGSY roads may simultaneously benefit from rural electrification or drinking-water schemes, complicating attribution.
questions.question: Many villages that received PMGSY roads may also have simultaneously benefited from rural electrification or drinking-water schemes. Why does this overlap complicate an impact evaluation that tries to attribute income or welfare changes specifically to PMGSY?
options: Because it becomes difficult to separate PMGSY's specific contribution to observed changes from the effects of the other concurrent interventions occurring in the same villages
Because it makes it impossible for any village to ever receive more than one government scheme
Because concurrent schemes always cancel out each other's effects entirely, leaving a net-zero impact to measure
Because it means PMGSY itself could not have had any road-construction activity in those villages
questions.explanation: When multiple schemes reach the same villages around the same time, isolating any one scheme's specific contribution to observed changes becomes harder -- a classic attribution challenge in impact evaluation. It doesn't mean villages can't receive multiple schemes, doesn't imply the effects cancel out, and doesn't affect whether PMGSY's own construction activity happened.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using PMGSY baseline data needs
questions.source_excerpt: Documenting a habitation's pre-construction status provides the reference point needed for later impact comparisons.
questions.question: Why would it matter for future PMGSY impact evaluations that baseline data (e.g. a habitation's income, school attendance, or market access before road construction) be collected prior to a road being built?
options: Without a documented pre-intervention baseline, there is no reliable starting point against which to measure how much things changed after the road was built
Baseline data has no bearing on measuring change over time
Baseline data is only useful if collected after the intervention is already complete
Baseline data collection is required only for schemes unrelated to infrastructure
questions.explanation: A pre-intervention baseline is the reference point against which any later change is measured -- without it, there is no reliable way to know how much things actually changed. Baseline data is valuable precisely because it is collected before the intervention, and this logic applies broadly, not only to non-infrastructure schemes.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using road maintenance and sustained impact
questions.source_excerpt: The sustainability of a road's condition affects whether an initial positive impact on connectivity-related outcomes persists.
questions.question: If a road built under PMGSY falls into disrepair a few years after construction due to inadequate maintenance, what does this imply about interpreting any initially observed positive impact (e.g., a short-term rise in market visits)?
options: The initial positive impact could fade or reverse over time, so a credible impact evaluation should consider how sustained the intervention (and its effects) actually are, not just an early snapshot
The initial positive impact is guaranteed to be permanent regardless of the road's later condition
Maintenance quality has no relationship to whether a connectivity-based impact persists over time
Once any positive impact is observed once, no further evaluation is ever needed
questions.explanation: If connectivity later degrades due to poor maintenance, an initially positive impact may not persist -- sound impact evaluation should therefore look at sustainability over time, not just an early snapshot, since maintenance quality directly affects whether the connectivity (and its benefits) endures.

questions.locator: Document's institutional background -- DMEO's independence
questions.source_excerpt: DMEO was structured as an independent evaluation office, formed by merging the Programme Evaluation Organisation and Independent Evaluation Office, rather than being run directly by the implementing ministry.
questions.question: DMEO was structured as an 'independent' evaluation office rather than being run directly by the ministry implementing PMGSY. Why does this independence matter for the credibility of impact findings?
options: An evaluator with some distance from the implementing ministry is less likely to face pressure to report favourable results, improving the credibility of its impact conclusions
Independence has no bearing on how credible an evaluation's findings are perceived to be
Independent evaluators are legally barred from ever reporting positive findings about a scheme
Independence means the evaluator cannot access any data about the scheme it is evaluating
questions.explanation: An evaluator with structural distance from the implementing ministry is less prone to conflict-of-interest pressure to produce favourable findings, strengthening the credibility of its impact assessments -- independence does not bar positive findings when warranted, nor does it cut off the evaluator's access to programme data it needs to do its job.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using a with-and-without design
questions.source_excerpt: Comparing currently connected habitations to otherwise-similar unconnected ones at the same point in time is a 'with-and-without' comparison design.
questions.question: Instead of a before-after comparison, an evaluator could compare currently-connected habitations against otherwise-similar, still-unconnected habitations at the same point in time -- a 'with-and-without' design. What is the main benefit of this approach over a simple before-after comparison?
options: By comparing two groups at the same point in time, it helps control for common time-varying factors (like a shared monsoon or a shared economic trend) that would otherwise confound a before-after comparison of a single village
It requires comparing a village only to itself, exactly as a before-after design does
It eliminates any need to find habitations that are otherwise similar to each other
It can only be used for evaluating urban, not rural, connectivity schemes
questions.explanation: Comparing connected and unconnected habitations at the same time point helps net out shared time-varying influences that a single village's before-after comparison cannot separate from the road's own effect. It is a genuinely different design from before-after, does require finding otherwise-comparable habitations, and applies equally in principle to rural connectivity contexts like PMGSY.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using access vs welfare outcomes
questions.source_excerpt: Improved physical access to a market or clinic does not automatically translate into improved household welfare outcomes.
questions.question: Why might an impact evaluation of PMGSY need to separately assess 'access' outcomes (e.g., can residents physically reach a market or clinic more easily) from 'welfare' outcomes (e.g., did household income or health actually improve)?
options: Because improved access is a necessary step but does not automatically guarantee that welfare gains follow -- other constraints (cost, information, demand) could still prevent access from translating into better outcomes
Because access and welfare outcomes are, by definition, exactly the same thing and never need separate measurement
Because welfare outcomes always improve automatically the moment physical access improves, with no exceptions
Because access outcomes are impossible to measure in any rural connectivity evaluation
questions.explanation: Physical access is often a necessary but not sufficient condition for welfare gains -- other barriers such as affordability, awareness, or demand-side constraints can prevent improved access from translating into actual income or health improvements, which is why evaluators track both separately.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using rapid vs panel data collection
questions.source_excerpt: A quick evaluation is more likely to rely on rapid household or administrative data collection than on a long-running panel survey.
questions.question: A 'quick' evaluation is more likely to rely on rapid household or administrative data collection than on a long-running panel survey tracking the same households over many years. What trade-off does this represent for impact evaluation?
options: Faster, lighter data collection speeds up delivery of findings but generally sacrifices some statistical power and the ability to track the same units' changes over a long period
There is no trade-off at all -- rapid data collection is strictly superior to long-panel surveys in every respect
Rapid data collection always produces more statistically powerful results than a multi-year panel survey
Administrative data can never be used for any impact evaluation purpose
questions.explanation: Rapid data collection methods deliver findings faster but typically involve smaller samples or single time-points, sacrificing the statistical power and long-run tracking a multi-year panel survey would offer -- a genuine trade-off, not a strict superiority in either direction, and administrative data remains a legitimate, if limited, input for impact assessment.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using PMGSY's prioritisation criteria
questions.source_excerpt: PMGSY has prioritised connecting larger and certain specific-category (hill, desert, tribal, conflict-affected) habitations first, rather than connecting all habitations at random.
questions.question: PMGSY has prioritised connecting larger and more specific-category habitations (e.g., certain hill, desert, tribal or conflict-affected areas) first. If an evaluator simply compares all already-connected habitations to all not-yet-connected ones nationally, what selection-bias risk arises?
options: The two groups may differ systematically in ways related to the prioritisation criteria themselves (e.g. size or terrain), so any observed outcome difference could reflect those pre-existing differences rather than the road's true causal effect
No selection-bias risk exists, since which habitations get connected first is entirely random
Selection bias only affects urban infrastructure evaluations, never rural road programmes
The prioritisation criteria guarantee that connected and unconnected habitations are always statistically identical
questions.explanation: Because connection was not random but based on criteria like population size and category, a national comparison of all connected versus all unconnected habitations risks conflating the road's effect with pre-existing differences tied to those very selection criteria -- a textbook selection-bias problem, not confined to urban settings, and not eliminated by the existence of prioritisation rules, which is precisely the source of the bias.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using how findings should be interpreted
questions.source_excerpt: A quick concurrent evaluation's findings are best treated as early, directional evidence rather than a definitive impact verdict.
questions.question: How should policymakers appropriately interpret the findings of a 'quick concurrent evaluation' of PMGSY, given its speed-oriented design?
options: As early, directional evidence useful for identifying implementation issues and enabling course correction, rather than as a definitive, final verdict on the programme's long-term impact
As the single, final, unchallengeable word on PMGSY's long-term impact, requiring no further evaluation
As having no practical use for policymaking whatsoever
As applicable only to programmes outside the rural development sector
questions.explanation: Given its speed-oriented, concurrent design, such an evaluation is best treated as early, directional evidence for course correction -- not a final, definitive impact verdict, but also not something without practical value, and its logic applies to the rural road programme it was designed to study.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using variation across overlapping schemes
questions.source_excerpt: Where habitations received different combinations of concurrent schemes, comparing across those combinations can help isolate a single scheme's contribution.
questions.question: Given that rural transformation often results from multiple concurrent schemes (roads, electrification, water supply) rather than any single one, what evaluation-design step can help better isolate PMGSY's specific contribution?
options: Explicitly comparing habitations that received PMGSY roads but not the other concurrent schemes against habitations that received the other schemes but not PMGSY, where such variation exists
Assuming that any observed change is automatically caused entirely by PMGSY, regardless of what else changed
Refusing to evaluate any village that also received another government scheme
Concluding that isolating any single scheme's effect is always completely impossible, so no attempt should ever be made
questions.explanation: Where variation exists in which combination of schemes different habitations received, comparing across those different combinations can help isolate PMGSY's own contribution -- a more careful design than either assuming full attribution to PMGSY alone or giving up on attribution entirely by excluding overlapping villages.

questions.locator: General impact-evaluation concept illustrated using complementary evaluation timelines
questions.source_excerpt: A quick concurrent evaluation and a later rigorous impact evaluation with matched comparison groups serve complementary purposes.
questions.question: How does a 'quick concurrent evaluation' of PMGSY relate to a later, more rigorous ex-post impact evaluation that might use matched comparison groups and multi-year outcome data?
options: The two are complementary -- the quick evaluation offers early operational feedback, while the later rigorous evaluation is better positioned to establish credible long-term causal impact
The quick evaluation makes any later rigorous impact evaluation entirely redundant
The two evaluation types are functionally identical and interchangeable in every respect
A rigorous ex-post evaluation must always be conducted before any concurrent evaluation is attempted
questions.explanation: A quick concurrent evaluation and a later rigorous impact evaluation serve complementary purposes -- fast operational feedback versus credible long-term causal attribution -- rather than one making the other redundant, being interchangeable, or requiring a fixed sequencing where the rigorous one must always come first.

questions.locator: Synthesis question drawing on the document's evaluation-design challenges
questions.source_excerpt: A credible causal assessment of PMGSY's long-term impact would combine a documented baseline, a credible comparison group, and outcome data timed to allow downstream effects to emerge.
questions.question: Drawing on the challenges above (counterfactual estimation, selection bias, attribution amid concurrent schemes, and time lags), which evaluation design would best support a credible assessment of PMGSY's causal impact on household income several years after road construction?
options: A design using pre-construction baseline data, a matched or rule-based comparison group of otherwise-similar unconnected habitations, and outcome data collected long enough after construction for downstream effects to materialise
A single post-construction survey of only the connected habitations, with no comparison group and no baseline data
A one-week data collection exercise conducted immediately after roads are declared complete
A design that ignores any habitations that also received other rural development schemes, discarding all available data on them
questions.explanation: Combining a documented pre-intervention baseline, a credible comparison group (matched or based on a rule like the population-threshold cutoff), and outcome measurement timed to allow downstream effects to emerge is the strongest available design among these options -- unlike a single post-hoc survey with no comparison or baseline, an immediate one-week snapshot too early to catch downstream effects, or discarding informative data on habitations that also received other schemes, which could instead be used to help isolate PMGSY's own contribution.
